t:
(a) In General.—Not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, the Secretary shall conduct a comprehensive analysis on the need for crashworthiness standards on property-carrying commercial motor vehicles with a gross vehicle weight rating or gross vehicle weight of at least 26,001 pounds involved in interstate commerce, including an evaluation of the need for 
roof strength, pillar strength, air bags, and other occupant protections standards, and frontal and back wall standards. 
    (b) Report.—Not later than 90 days after completing the comprehensive analysis under subsection (a), the Secretary shall report the results of the analysis and any recommendations to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation of the Senate and the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure of the House of Representatives.

fable.w: The section directs the Secretary to conduct an internal analysis of crashworthiness standards and report the results to congressional committees. The tempting reading is that the report and recommendations are a formal consultative process, but Congress is inside the federal government, so nothing crosses the federal boundary. No comment period, rulemaking, hearing, advisory committee, or consultation with states, industry, or the public is required.
fable.s: the Secretary shall report the results of the analysis and any recommendations to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation of the Senate and the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure of the House of Representatives.

qwen_block.w: The section requires the Secretary to conduct an analysis and submit a report to congressional committees. Congress is part of the federal government, so reporting to it is an internal government action, not participation by outside parties. There is no requirement for public comment, consultation with states or tribes, or involvement of an advisory board with non-federal members.
qwen_block.s: the Secretary shall report the results of the analysis and any recommendations to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation of the Senate and the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure of the House of Representatives.

opus.w: The section requires only an internal analysis by the Secretary and a report to congressional committees, which are inside the federal government. No outside party (states, industry, experts, or the public) is consulted, and there is no comment period, hearing, rulemaking authority, or right to sue. The report and 'recommendations' language looks procedural, but it never crosses the federal boundary.
opus.s: the Secretary shall report the results of the analysis and any recommendations to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation of the Senate and the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure of the House of Representatives
opus.b:
I'm calling this section a **No**: it involves no participation by anyone outside the federal government.

1. **The tempting reading:** The section has formal, procedural-sounding steps. There is a "comprehensive analysis," "recommendations," and a report to two congressional committees, which could look like participation. That reading fails because every actor named is inside the federal government: the Secretary and the committees of Congress. No states, industry, experts or members of the public are consulted. There is no comment period, hearing, rulemaking authority or right to sue.

qwen_chat.w: The section requires the Secretary to conduct an analysis and submit a report to congressional committees. Congress is part of the federal government, so reporting to it is internal government communication, not participation with outside parties. There is no requirement to consult with states, tribes, the public, or other non-federal entities.
qwen_chat.s: Not later than 90 days after completing the comprehensive analysis under subsection (a), the Secretary shall report the results of the analysis and any recommendations to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation of the Senate and the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure of the House of Representatives.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the "comprehensive analysis" implies gathering data from outside experts or the public, thus constituting participation. However, the text does not mandate any such consultation; it only mandates the Secretary conduct an analysis and report it. The report is sent to Congress, which is inside the federal government. Therefore, there is no required interaction with outside parties.
